## Purpose

This SOP describes the procedures for obtaining site access and
research permits for field work conducted by the EA Program. Field
research on public or institutional lands almost always requires
advance authorization, and working without proper permits can result
in fines, confiscation of samples, invalidation of data, and
jeopardized relationships with land managers. This document provides
an agency-by-agency guide covering the landowners and managers most
commonly encountered by EA Program researchers.


## Scope

- **Applies to:** All EA Program field activities that take place on
  lands managed by the agencies and institutions listed in this SOP,
  including class field trips, independent student research, and
  faculty-led projects
- **Does not apply to:** Laboratory procedures; field work on private
  land (which requires landowner permission negotiated on a
  case-by-case basis); marine or offshore research (which may require
  additional permits from NOAA or the California Coastal Commission)
- **Key principle:** It is the responsibility of the PI (or the
  supervising faculty member) to determine what permits are required
  and to obtain all necessary approvals before any field work begins.
  Students should never assume that their faculty advisor has obtained
  permits -- always confirm.


## Responsibilities

| Role              | Responsibility                                          |
|:------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|
| PI / Faculty      | Identify required permits, submit applications, maintain permit files, ensure compliance with all conditions |
| Field Lead        | Carry copies of active permits in the field; confirm permit status before each outing |
| Students          | Verify that permits are in place before field work; follow all permit conditions; report any compliance issues to the PI |


## General Principles

### Planning Timeline

Permit processing times vary widely. As a general rule, submit
applications at least 60--90 days before the planned start of field
work. Some agencies (particularly federal ones involving NEPA review
or listed species) may require 6 months or more. The table below
provides typical lead times; always confirm with the specific office.

| Agency / Institution       | Typical Lead Time      |
|:---------------------------|:-----------------------|
| Bernard Field Station      | 1--2 weeks             |
| California State Parks     | 60--90 days            |
| UC Natural Reserve System  | 2--4 weeks             |
| CDFW (General Use SCP)     | 60--90 days            |
| CDFW (Specific Use SCP)    | 3--6 months            |
| USFWS (Section 10)         | 3--12 months           |
| BLM                        | 60--120 days           |
| National Park Service      | 60--120 days           |
| USDA Forest Service        | 60--120 days           |

### Permits You May Need Simultaneously

A single field project can require permits from multiple agencies. For
example, sampling macroinvertebrates in a stream within a National
Forest may require a USFS Special Use Permit, a CDFW Scientific
Collecting Permit, and (if listed species are present) a USFWS
Section 10 permit. The land management agency will typically not
finalize its own permit until copies of all other required permits are
submitted.

### Permit Files

The PI must maintain a digital folder (in the EA Program Google Drive
or GitHub repository) containing:

- Copies of all active permits (signed, final versions)
- Copies of all applications submitted
- Copies of annual reports and compliance documents submitted to
  agencies
- Expiration dates and renewal deadlines

Field leads must carry printed or digital copies of relevant permits
during every field outing.

### Insurance and Liability

Several agencies require proof of liability insurance as a condition
of permit issuance. Pomona College maintains institutional liability
coverage; contact the Office of Risk Management to obtain a
Certificate of Insurance naming the specific agency as an additional
insured party.


## Agency-Specific Procedures

### Robert J. Bernard Biological Field Station (BFS)

The BFS is an 86-acre facility of The Claremont Colleges located at
1400 N. Amherst Avenue, Claremont, CA. Access requires advance
approval from the BFS Director.

**When a permit is needed:** All research projects, class field trips,
and organized activities on the BFS require a Use Request, even for
Claremont Colleges faculty and students. Casual, unaccompanied
pedestrian access also requires prior authorization.

**How to apply:**

1. Contact the BFS Director (Dr. Wallace M. Meyer III,
   wallace.meyer\@pomona.edu, 909-621-8577) to discuss the proposed
   project
2. Submit the appropriate online Use Request Form at
   <https://bfs.sites.pomona.edu/using-the-bfs/apply-to-use/>:
   - **Research Request Form** -- for all research projects
     (including independent study and thesis research)
   - **Course Request Form** -- for class field trips
   - **Other Use Request Form** -- for community groups, outreach,
     and non-research activities
3. Await approval from the BFS Director before beginning any work

**Special conditions:**

- The BFS is not a recreational park. All users must follow the BFS
  Rules for Use, including staying on designated paths except when
  conducting approved research
- Multiple ongoing research projects may overlap spatially; coordinate
  with the BFS Director to avoid conflicts
- If your research involves listed or sensitive species (e.g., coastal
  California gnatcatcher habitat in the sage scrub), you may also need
  a CDFW Scientific Collecting Permit and/or USFWS authorization (see
  Sections 5.4 and 5.5)
- Provide a summary of findings to the BFS Director upon project
  completion

**Website:** <https://bfs.sites.pomona.edu/>

### California Department of Parks and Recreation (State Parks)

California State Parks requires a Scientific Research and Collecting
Permit (form DPR 65) for most scientific activities conducted within
the State Park System, including field work, specimen collection, and
systematic data collection intended for publication.

**When a permit is needed:** If you intend to collect specimens or
data and/or produce a written document of your findings (thesis,
paper, report), a permit is required.

**How to apply:**

1. Download and complete form DPR 65 from
   <https://www.parks.ca.gov/?page_id=21557>
2. Prepare a full study proposal following the Study Proposal
   Guidelines for Research in California State Parks
3. Submit the application, study proposal, proof of insurance, and
   copies of any other required permits (CDFW, USFWS, etc.) to the
   appropriate State Parks district office or, for multi-district
   projects, to the Natural Resources Division in Sacramento at
   nrd.research\@parks.ca.gov
4. Allow 60--90 days for processing. Projects involving soil
   disturbance, sensitive resources, or sensitive areas may take
   longer

**Conditions and reporting:**

- Collecting is limited to what is necessary for the approved project;
  collected materials may not be used for commercial profit
- The PI must submit a summary report of activities and findings to
  State Parks, and renewal is contingent on receipt of this report
- All work must be conducted in a manner that minimizes impact on park
  resources, away from roads, trails, and developed areas when
  feasible

**Website:** <https://www.parks.ca.gov/?page_id=21557>

### University of California Natural Reserve System (UCNRS)

The UCNRS manages 41+ reserves across California representing most
major state ecosystems. Unlike state and national parks, the reserves
are not open to recreational use; they exist specifically for
research, teaching, and public service.

**When a permit is needed:** All research projects and class visits
require an approved application through the Reserve Application
Management System (RAMS).

**How to apply:**

1. Contact the reserve director(s) of the site(s) you wish to use to
   discuss project requirements and suitability
2. Review the NRS Use Guidelines at
   <https://ucnrs.org/reserve-research-guidelines/>
3. Submit a research application through RAMS at
   <https://rams.ucnrs.org>
4. Once the application is approved by the reserve director, submit a
   Reservation for each planned visit through RAMS
5. Download and submit reserve waivers of liability as required

**Special conditions:**

- IACUC approval is required if the project involves vertebrate
  animals; copies must be submitted before work begins
- Additional agency permits (CDFW, USFWS) may be required depending
  on the species and activities involved
- The NRS prohibits activities that translocate non-native genotypes
  to or from NRS sites
- Facility rates vary by reserve; day use is free at most reserves
- All equipment and infrastructure must be removed and sites restored
  at the conclusion of each project

**Website:** <https://ucnrs.org/>

### California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW)

CDFW issues Scientific Collecting Permits (SCPs) for the take or
possession of wildlife (mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish,
certain plants, and invertebrates) for scientific, educational, and
propagation purposes.

**When a permit is needed:** Any time your research involves
capturing, handling, marking, or collecting wildlife -- or when there
is potential for incidental take of sensitive species. "Take" under
California Fish and Game Code Section 86 means to hunt, pursue, catch,
capture, or kill, or attempt to do so.

**Permit types:**

- **General Use SCP** -- for more common species, non-invasive
  methods, and areas outside Marine Protected Areas. Issued for inland
  fisheries (DFW 1379GF), marine (DFW 1379GM), or terrestrial
  wildlife (DFW 1379GW)
- **Specific Use SCP** -- for focused studies involving prohibited
  wildlife, more invasive methods, or sensitive locations including
  MPAs (form DFW 1379S)

**How to apply:**

1. Review the SCP regulations (Title 14, Section 650, CCR) and
   Standard Conditions at
   <https://wildlife.ca.gov/Licensing/Scientific-Collecting>
2. Apply online through the Scientific Collecting Permit Portal (SCPP)
3. Pay the required permit fee before issuance

**Additional authorizations that may be needed:**

- **CESA-listed species** (threatened, endangered, or candidate under
  the California Endangered Species Act): requires a separate CESA
  Memorandum of Understanding from the appropriate CDFW review program
- **Fully Protected species**: requires a Fully Protected MOU
- **Federally listed species**: requires a federal ESA authorization
  (see Section 5.5)

**Reporting:** Each permitholder must submit a Mandatory Wildlife
Report (form DFW 1379a) annually.

**Website:** <https://wildlife.ca.gov/Licensing/Scientific-Collecting>

### U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS)

USFWS administers permits for activities involving species listed
under the federal Endangered Species Act (ESA), migratory birds
(Migratory Bird Treaty Act), and wildlife on National Wildlife
Refuges.

**When a permit is needed:**

- Any research involving take (including capture, handling, or
  harassment) of federally listed threatened or endangered species
  requires a Section 10(a)(1)(A) recovery permit
- Research involving migratory birds (banding, capture, nest
  monitoring) requires a federal Bird Banding Permit and/or Scientific
  Collecting Permit
- Research conducted on National Wildlife Refuge lands requires a
  Special Use Permit from the refuge manager

**How to apply:**

1. For ESA-listed species: submit form 3-200-55 (Scientific Purposes,
   Enhancement of Propagation or Survival) through the USFWS
   Endangered Species permits portal
2. For migratory birds: apply through the USFWS Bird Banding
   Laboratory or the federal permits portal
3. For refuge access: contact the specific refuge manager to discuss
   the project and obtain a Special Use Permit

**Key considerations:**

- Section 10 permit applications are subject to Federal Register
  notice and a 30-day public comment period
- Processing times are long (3--12 months); plan well ahead
- Under federal law, specimens collected remain federal property
- Annual reports are required for all active permits

**Website:** <https://www.fws.gov/service/apply-permit>

---

### Bureau of Land Management (BLM)

BLM manages extensive public lands in California, including desert,
grassland, and mountain areas where EA Program research may occur.

**When a permit is needed:** Any organized research activity on
BLM-managed lands, including specimen collection, installation of
monitoring equipment, and systematic surveys, requires coordination
with the local BLM Field Office.

**How to apply:**

1. Contact the nearest BLM Field Office to discuss the proposed
   research. A directory is available at <https://www.blm.gov/office/directory>
2. BLM staff will determine whether a formal Special Recreation
   Permit, a research authorization, or another type of approval is
   needed
3. Submit the required application materials, including maps, project
   descriptions, and copies of any other agency permits (CDFW, USFWS)
4. Allow 60--120 days for processing; complex projects requiring NEPA
   analysis may take longer

**Special conditions:**

- Casual collecting of common invertebrate and plant fossils is
  allowed without a permit under the Paleontological Resources
  Preservation Act, but vertebrate fossil collection always requires a
  permit
- Research on BLM lands involving listed species will require
  coordination with USFWS or NMFS under ESA Section 7
- Researchers are encouraged to share findings with BLM staff

**Website:** <https://www.blm.gov/learn/science-in-the-blm/conducting-science>

---

### National Park Service (NPS)

NPS requires a Scientific Research and Collecting Permit for most
scientific activities related to natural or social science resources
in any unit of the National Park System.

**When a permit is needed:** If you propose any study in the natural
sciences (biology, geology, physics) or social sciences (visitor
surveys, education research) within a national park, monument,
seashore, or other NPS unit, you need a permit.

**How to apply:**

1. Create an investigator account in the Research Permit and Reporting
   System (RPRS) at <https://irma.nps.gov/rprs/>
2. Locate the park profile in RPRS (Search > Parks) to find the
   research coordinator's contact information and any park-specific
   conditions
3. Submit a complete application and research proposal through RPRS
4. The park's research coordinator will review the application, and a
   draft permit will be prepared for your review. The final permit
   must be signed by both the investigator and a park official

**Conditions and reporting:**

- A printed copy of the signed permit must be carried during all field
  work inside the park
- Investigator Annual Reports (IARs) must be submitted through RPRS
  every year the permit is active
- Copies of final reports, publications, and other products must be
  provided to the park
- Specimens collected remain federal property under NPS authority;
  repository arrangements must be specified in the permit application
- Failure to submit IARs may result in denial of future permits

**Website:** <https://www.nps.gov/subjects/science/research-permit.htm>

---

### USDA Forest Service (USFS)

National Forests are managed for multiple use, and a permit is
required to conduct research on Forest Service-managed lands.

**When a permit is needed:** Any research activity on National Forest
System (NFS) lands, including collection of plants or animals,
installation of equipment, and systematic surveys. Some low-impact
observational studies may qualify for a Research Permit Waiver at the
discretion of the local forest staff.

**How to apply:**

1. Contact the Ranger District office for the National Forest where
   you plan to work. For Southern California, relevant forests include
   the San Bernardino, Angeles, Cleveland, and Los Padres National
   Forests
2. Download and complete a Research Special-Use Operating
   Plan/Itinerary from the forest's website and email it to the
   district permit coordinator
3. Forest staff will determine whether a full Special Use Permit or a
   Research Permit Waiver is appropriate
4. Applications undergo initial screening and may require NEPA
   analysis; allow 60--120 days for processing

**Special conditions:**

- Projects involving wildlife or threatened/endangered plants may
  require additional authorization from CDFW and/or USFWS (ESA
  Section 7 consultation)
- A summary of findings (theses, papers, reports) must be provided to
  the Forest Service upon completion
- Equipment left on NFS lands must be authorized under the permit and
  removed at project conclusion

**Website:** <https://www.fs.usda.gov/> (navigate to the specific
National Forest's permits page)


## Permit Decision Flowchart

Use the following steps to determine what permits you need:

1. **Identify the land manager.** Who owns or manages the land where
   you will work? (BFS, State Parks, UCNRS, BLM, NPS, USFS, private,
   etc.)
2. **Obtain the land access permit** from the land manager (Sections
   5.1--5.8 above).
3. **Will you handle, capture, collect, or disturb wildlife?** If yes,
   you likely need a CDFW Scientific Collecting Permit (Section 5.4).
4. **Are any federally listed species present at your site, or could
   they be incidentally encountered?** If yes, you likely need a
   USFWS Section 10 permit or ESA Section 7 consultation through the
   land management agency (Section 5.5).
5. **Are any state-listed species (CESA) present?** If yes, you need a
   CESA MOU from CDFW in addition to your SCP (Section 5.4).
6. **Does the land manager require proof of other agency permits
   before issuing its own?** If yes, obtain the other permits first
   and submit copies with your land access application.

::: {.callout-tip}
### When in doubt, ask

If you are unsure whether a permit is required, contact the agency.
It is always better to ask in advance than to be stopped in the field
or to have your data and specimens invalidated.
:::

## Training Record

Before leading field work on any permitted site, personnel must:

1. Read this SOP in full
2. Identify all permits required for their specific project and site
3. Confirm with the PI that all permits are active and in hand
4. Know where to find copies of active permits (digital and/or printed)
5. Understand the reporting requirements for each active permit
6. Be signed off by the PI or designated field lead
